The elongate tigerfish, Hydrocynus forskahlii, is a large-bodied African characin that attains a remarkable maximum adult size. Field surveys and capture records indicate that the species can reach an ultimate total length of 78 cm [Li = 78 cm], a dimension that places it among the largest members of the genus Hydrocynus and reflects its role as a top predator in riverine ecosystems across its sub-Saharan range. The hatchling emerges from the pelagic egg at a remarkably diminutive size; based on an egg diameter of 1.1 mm, the calculated wet weight at birth is approximately 0.00069 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00069 grams]. This minute initial mass is consistent with the small, buoyant eggs typical of many freshwater characiforms and underscores the substantial ontogenetic growth trajectory the species must undergo to achieve its imposing adult dimensions.

Sexual maturation in Hydrocynus forskahlii occurs at a comparatively modest body length relative to the species' ultimate size. Mark-recapture studies and gonadal inspections have established that individuals attain puberty at a total length of 20 cm [Lp = 20 cm], indicating that the onset of reproductive capability is reached well before somatic growth is complete. This early maturation relative to maximum size is a life-history strategy that likely enhances lifetime reproductive output in a variable environment. At a stable water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], embryonic development proceeds rapidly; the time from fertilization to egg hatching, or age at birth, is just 4.5 days [ab = 4.5 days]. This short incubation period is common among tropical cypriniforms and characiforms, allowing the vulnerable yolk-sac larva to emerge quickly from the demersal egg environment.

Reproductive output in the elongate tigerfish has been characterized through comparative analyses with the closely related tigerfish, Hydrocynus vittatus. At the typical thermal regime of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], estimates for a female at a body weight of 1.7 kg indicate that fecundity per spawning event is roughly 342,000 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = roughly 342,000 eggs per clutch], and the species is believed to produce approximately 0.25 clutches each year [F_R_i = approximately 0.25 clutches each year]. This exceptionally high fecundity is a hallmark of many large, iteroparous freshwater teleosts, offsetting the high mortality rates experienced by pelagic eggs and early larvae. The combination of a massive single clutch size and a relatively infrequent spawning interval still maximizes the number of offspring a female can contribute over a single breeding season.

The ultimate wet weight documented for adult Hydrocynus forskahlii is based on the maximum published weight recorded for the species. Available records indicate that adults attain an asymptotic body mass of approximately 6.9 kilograms [Wwi = approximately 6.9 kilograms], a value that confirms the species' status as a heavyweight among African characins. Experiments conducted under controlled conditions at 28 °C [T = 28 °C] have allowed researchers to observe the species' complete lifespan from the yolk-dependent larva through the sexually mature adult. Such captive studies, corroborated by analysis of growth increments in wild specimens, suggest that the maximum lifespan, or longevity, of Hydrocynus forskahlii reaches approximately 7 years [am = approximately 7 years] when maintained at 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. This lifespan is typical for a predator of its size in equatorial freshwater systems.

The elongate tigerfish occupies the role of an apex predator in the rivers and lakes of the Congo Basin and Lake Tanganyika, where it exerts strong top-down control on prey fish communities. Stable isotope analyses indicate that Hydrocynus forskahlii feeds primarily on large cyprinids and cichlids, with individuals above 30 cm total length showing a marked ontogenetic shift toward piscivory. Juvenile tigerfish, by contrast, rely heavily on macroinvertebrates and small zooplankton during their first few months after the exotrophic transition. Seasonal flooding patterns trigger mass spawning aggregations in the upper reaches of river systems, where females deposit their demersal eggs among submerged vegetation. Larval growth is rapid under the warm, food-rich conditions of the flooded plains, with young-of-year individuals reaching up to 12 cm by the end of the first dry season. This combination of fast early growth, early maturation, and high fecundity has allowed Hydrocynus forskahlii to maintain stable populations across its range despite intensive commercial fishing pressure in certain areas.
